Academic-integrity workshop: a student’s draft plan and the intervention.

STUDENT’S DRAFT

“Put the formula strip behind the calculator cover. Keep the regular phone in the collection envelope and use an older device for a one-character message. Two taps on the desk mean look at question three; touching the bottle means send the letter, not the explanation. Sit where the proctor’s route leaves a blind angle, and ask for a restroom break only after enough time has passed to make the absence look ordinary. If the friend receives a different test version, compare topics rather than reading answers aloud.”

ADVISER’S NOTE: This is a prohibited plan, not study advice. It names concealment, an unauthorized device, coded communication, and an attempt to exploit a break. The workshop preserves the text because students and instructors need to recognize the warning signs, but the plan is not reliable and should never be used. A room check, changed seating, numbered scratch paper, device logs, a missed signal, or matching unusual errors can expose the arrangement. Academic-integrity staff may review the paper inventory, seating chart, platform records, and messages.

STUDENT: I am tempted because I am behind, but I do not want one exam to become a disciplinary case.

ADVISER: Make the remaining time useful. Divide the syllabus into can explain, partly understand, and cannot yet solve. Work first on the middle category. Close the notes, retrieve each principle from memory, solve a representative problem, compare the result with the source, and record the misconception. Ask the instructor or teaching assistant what is in scope, use tutoring or a small retrieval-practice group, and contact the accessibility office before the test if illness, disability, anxiety, or caregiving affects preparation.

During the exam, bring only permitted materials, read the rules, budget time, begin with questions you know, show legitimate work, and return to uncertain items later. If a fact is forgotten, reason from related principles rather than reaching for unauthorized help. If prohibited material has already been brought, do not use it; follow the course’s process for putting it away or notifying the proctor.
